text.p: Copper prices surged on Tuesday as inventories fell to fresh six-year lows amid fears that output could be hurt in the world's biggest producer Chile.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau index fell 0.23 points to 240.64.

Prices for delivery in three months touched the highest level in 2-1/2 months at $2,057 after stocks in London Metal Exchange (LME) warehouses continued a series of falls. LME stocks eroded by 4,225 tonnes to 109,175 tonnes, the lowest level since August 1990. The premium for prompt metal soared as traders scrambled for material, rising to nearly $100.

Many analysts, however, were perplexed since the price rise is still much below the year's peak around $2,715 in May. Prices ended $33 stronger at $2,045 per tonne. "It is very hard to make sense of this. It looks like somebody is trying to keep it in a range," a senior trader said. Some analysts believe stocks are not being consumed but moved out of LME warehouses into hidden stockpiles. "Traders continue to smell a rat and remain very wary about putting too much trust into the LME stock erosion," an analyst said. The market was watching closely developments in central Chile where the worst drought in 30 years threatened the water-dependent copper processing industry.
Aluminium was only slightly stronger, closing $6.50 firmer at $1,454.50 per tonne.

Gold probed slightly higher levels on Tuesday, although it was struggling to build on gains posted at the start of the week, London dealers said. Platinum and palladium were also hanging on to recent gains, while silver prices backed down from early highs. Gold bullion fixed at $381.90 an ounce, its highest fixing since October 29, versus $381.60 in the morning and a London close on Monday of $380.50/$381.00.

CBOT wheat futures were strongly higher at midsession on a cut by USDA in its estimate for world and U.S. ending stocks, traders said. "World ending stocks were cut, U.S. stocks were cut and that prompted some to cover their shorts," said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for FIMAT Futures. USDA in its November production and supply/demand reports Tuesday trimmed to 435 million bushels from 470 million its estimate for 1996-97 U.S. wheat ending stocks. The 1996-97 U.S. marketing year is slated to end on May 31. USDA also cut its outlook for world wheat supplies. At 1123 CST, wheat was 1-1/4 to seven cents per bushel higher, with December up 6-1/2 at $3.90. March was up 4-1/2 at $3.83-1/2.

CSCE world sugar futures closed weaker but above session lows in what market sources saw as a gradual and continuing downtrend. A bout of late-session speculative selling pushed spot March closer to support at 10.29 cents a lb to a daily low of 10.35 cents. Prices recovered slightly from the lows by the close. March finished at 10.38, down 0.17, after trading from 10.48 to 10.35. The back months ended off 0.11 to 0.05.

The NYMEX oil complex was lower Tuesday afternoon but rangebound ahead of this evening's weekly oil inventory data by the American Petroleum Institute (API), traders said. "The volume is thin. Everyone is sidelined ahead of the APIs," said GSC Energy trader Al Lindseth. Lindseth said forecasts of moderating temperatures for the U.S. Northeast after Friday was weighing on prices. At 1401 EST, December crude was off 11 cents at $23.26 a barrel while December heating oil stood 0.10 cent lower at 68.25 cents a gallon.
